task.goal: Teach beginner gardeners to decide when to water seedlings using soil evidence rather than a fixed daily habit.
hard_constraints: A 35-minute indoor session with pots, soil, water and paper; no electronic moisture meter.
Avoid overwatering live shared seedlings during practice.
Include a dry/wet ambiguous case and an individual transfer decision with a reason and a follow-up observation.
task.available_resources: Prepared sample pots at different moisture levels.
task.expected_result: Hands-on activity and a safe decision check.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check beneath the surface: a depth-based decision routine
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is replacing the daily watering cue with a repeatable inspection of soil near the seedling’s roots. Learners practice three actions: inspect the surface, gently feel soil below it near the pot edge, and decide whether to water, wait, or gather more evidence. The instructor sets a suitable inspection depth for the seedlings being taught; beginners should not probe through roots.

Use prepared, unplanted sample pots containing comparable soil, including dry soil, moist soil, and an ambiguous pot with a dry-looking surface but moist soil underneath. Live shared seedlings remain observation-only. During minutes 0–5, ask learners whether they would water each pot based on appearance. During minutes 5–10, demonstrate the inspection routine and explain that visibly dry surface soil alone does not establish root-zone dryness. During minutes 10–22, learners inspect samples and record evidence and decisions on paper. They may add a small amount of water to a designated dry, unplanted sample and inspect how far it penetrates after several minutes.

During minutes 22–30, each learner independently assesses a previously unseen sample, records a decision, gives a soil-based reason, and specifies a follow-up observation. During minutes 30–35, they make that observation where feasible—for example, checking beneath a damp surface—and revise their decision if needed.

This requires prepared moisture contrasts, accessible soil, water, and paper. It assumes comparable soil and known seedling needs. Touch judgments are imperfect, and soil that feels wet cannot alone establish drainage quality. The intended outcome is a defensible inspection routine, not a universal moisture threshold.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare each learner’s initial appearance-only decision with their independent decision after instruction. Use a fresh ambiguous pot with a dry surface and moist lower soil, alongside a genuinely dry pot. The instructor checks lower-soil conditions directly before use. A minimal success signal is correctly withholding water in the ambiguous case while recognizing the dry case, with reasons citing inspected soil and a relevant follow-up. If learners still follow surface appearance or simply choose ‘wait’ for every pot, the routine has not demonstrated the intended discrimination.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Learn the pot’s water weight: calibrated lifting
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is learning that water changes the weight of an otherwise comparable pot. Learners calibrate their hands against dry and adequately moist reference pots, then use relative weight to trigger a watering decision or a closer soil check.

Prepare matching pots with equal amounts of the same soil: one dry reference, one moist but freely drained reference, and several intermediate samples. Include an ambiguous sample whose surface looks wet after a light sprinkling but whose lower soil remains dry. Use unplanted samples for all watering practice; shared live seedlings are observation-only.

During minutes 0–7, demonstrate lifting the two references and explain why pot size, soil quantity, and plant size must remain comparable. During minutes 7–17, learners lift and order intermediate pots by apparent water content, recording confidence on paper. They inspect soil below the surface afterward to check their ordering. During minutes 17–23, discuss the wet-looking but light pot: a light pot warrants checking the root zone, rather than assuming a damp surface means sufficient water.

During minutes 23–30, each learner independently assesses a new matching pot, chooses water, wait, or inspect further, and records a reason and follow-up observation. During minutes 30–35, they complete the check. If watering an unplanted practice pot, add water gradually, pause, then lift and inspect below the surface again.

Only prepared pots, soil, water, and paper are needed; no scale is required. This method assumes the weight contrast is perceptible and learners can lift safely. It may fail with heavy containers or small moisture differences. Reference weights must be relearned when container, soil, or plant size changes.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Before calibration, ask learners to judge two unfamiliar matching pots by appearance alone. After calibration, present a fresh pair: a wet-looking but internally dry pot and a sufficiently moist pot. Compare decisions and inspect lower soil to establish the prepared conditions. The method gains support if learners distinguish the pair using weight plus verification, and specify a useful follow-up such as rechecking depth after watering. If weight rankings are inconsistent or do not improve decisions over appearance alone, lifting is unsuitable as the primary cue for these pots.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make moisture visible with a calibrated paper-contact test
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is capillary transfer: soil releases some available water into absorbent paper, producing a visible damp patch. Learners compare that patch with locally prepared references instead of using the calendar as a watering cue. This differs from judging soil by appearance, touch, or pot weight.

Use matching unplanted sample pots containing the same soil and ordinary absorbent paper. Prepare dry, appropriately moist, and very wet references, plus an ambiguous pot with a wet surface over dry lower soil. The instructor must know the appropriate moisture range and root-zone location for the seedlings being discussed. All shared live seedlings remain observation-only; learners water only designated unplanted samples.

Minutes 0–6: learners make initial watering decisions from appearance. Minutes 6–12: demonstrate pressing equal-sized soil portions from the relevant depth onto identical paper pieces for the same duration and pressure. Compare the resulting damp patches against the references. A patch resembling the adequately moist reference supports waiting; resemblance to the dry reference supports watering under the stated seedling conditions. An unclear result calls for another sample, not automatic watering.

Minutes 12–22: learners test contrasting pots, including separate surface and lower-soil samples from the ambiguous case. Discuss why surface wetness can conceal insufficient moisture below.

Minutes 22–30: each learner independently tests an unfamiliar pot and records a decision, soil-based reason, and follow-up observation. Minutes 30–35: learners carry out that observation—for example, retesting another lower-soil location or checking moisture penetration after cautiously watering a dry practice pot.

This requires paper that visibly absorbs moisture and sufficiently distinct reference responses. Soil texture, paper type, pressure, and sample size affect transfer. The test is a local comparison, not a universal moisture measurement; if references cannot be distinguished, it is unsuitable.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First check whether identical paper tests visibly distinguish the dry and appropriately moist references. Failure falsifies the method’s practical usefulness for these materials. If they differ, compare learners’ appearance-only decisions with their independent paper-based decisions on a fresh wet-surface/dry-below pot and an adequately moist pot. Inspect the prepared lower soil to verify conditions. The method earns preliminary support only if learners distinguish both cases, cite the paper evidence, and complete a relevant follow-up; choosing water or wait for every pot does not pass.

EXPAND.title: Repair a watering rule through contrasting cases
EXPAND.proposal:
The main mechanism is learning by counterexample: learners test a proposed watering rule against soil evidence, explain its failures, and replace it with a conditional rule. The activity teaches decision reasoning without requiring beginners to perform a reliable moisture measurement themselves.

Prepare unplanted sample pots with contrasting moisture conditions. The instructor exposes soil from the depth relevant to the seedlings and identifies its condition using locally appropriate dry and adequately moist references. Include an ambiguous pot with a dry surface over moist lower soil. Shared live seedlings remain observation-only; water is used only on designated unplanted samples.

Minutes 0–5: present the paper rule, ‘Water every morning,’ and ask learners to predict its decisions for every pot. Minutes 5–12: reveal the soil evidence. Learners identify where the rule would add unnecessary water. Explain that seedling species, growing medium, drainage, and root development affect what counts as sufficiently moist.

Minutes 12–22: pairs inspect the samples and repair two proposed rules: ‘Water daily’ and ‘Water whenever the surface looks dry.’ Their replacement must explain when to water, when to wait, and what to inspect when evidence conflicts. They then exchange rules and look for a sample that exposes a weakness.

Minutes 22–30: each learner independently receives a previously unseen sample with instructor-exposed soil evidence. They record water, wait, or inspect further, a reason tied to that evidence, and a specific follow-up observation. Minutes 30–35: they perform the observation, such as examining a second location at the relevant depth, and revise their decision if warranted.

This requires prepared samples, water, paper, and an instructor able to interpret the soil for the seedlings concerned. Its limit is that reasoning from supplied evidence does not establish independent sampling skill. Success depends on learners explaining decisions rather than merely repeating the replacement rule.
EXPAND.experiment: For a small pilot, give one group the rule-repair activity and another a brief explanation of the same soil-based guidance, with equal practice time. Individually show both groups two unfamiliar samples: a dry-surface/moist-below case and a genuinely dry case. Compare decisions, evidence-based reasons, and relevant follow-up observations. The proposed advantage is unsupported if rule repair produces no clearer transfer, or if learners simply adopt ‘always wait.’ Keep every assessment observation-only or use unplanted pots.

REFINE.title: Repair candidate 0: require a second location when moisture evidence conflicts
REFINE.proposal:
Original candidate index: 0. This is the most promising candidate because direct inspection below the surface is feasible with the supplied materials and teaches evidence-based watering. Its consequential weakness is that one inspection near the pot edge can misrepresent unevenly moist soil, leaving “gather more evidence” without a concrete action. Preserve the depth-based routine, but require a second check at the same instructor-set depth on the opposite side whenever surface and deeper evidence conflict or the first check is uncertain. If the two deeper checks disagree, choose “inspect further” and withhold water pending instructor review; do not infer that the whole pot needs watering. This makes the ambiguous case actionable and reduces watering based on an unrepresentative spot.

Keep the original 35-minute indoor schedule: 0–5 appearance-only decisions; 5–10 demonstration; 10–22 sample practice; 22–30 individual transfer; 30–35 follow-up. Use only pots, soil, water and paper, with all probing and watering confined to unplanted samples; shared live seedlings remain observation-only. Each learner independently assesses an unseen sample, records water/wait/inspect further with a soil-based reason, and performs a follow-up observation. Prerequisites are comparable soil, enough prepared samples, and an instructor-selected inspection depth and suitable moisture reference for the seedlings. Remaining limit: two locations still cannot establish moisture throughout a pot.
REFINE.experiment: Prepare an unseen unplanted pot with a dry surface, dry soil at one inspection location and moist soil at the opposite location, plus a uniformly dry sample. Verify these conditions before use. The smallest falsifying check is whether a learner checks the second location in the conflicting case, records “inspect further” with the conflicting evidence as the reason, and follows up by checking another location with the instructor. The learner should also identify the uniformly dry sample as needing water under the stated seedling conditions. Watering the mixed sample from one dry reading, or withholding water from both without discrimination, fails the check.
